security_feature_bypassed: Truthful completion signalling across a security zeroize in the HMAC core. A zeroize is meant to leave the block claiming no valid result, so that a consumer cannot mistake post-zeroize output for a real authentication tag. The audited register block clears the FSM but keeps the tag-validity flag asserted, so the block continues to advertise a valid tag it no longer holds.
finding:
src/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv:181-209 is one always_ff named reg_update holding three registers. Its reset arm at :184-187 clears all three, including digest_valid_reg at :185. Its zeroize arm at :190-196 clears only hmac_ctrl_reg and hmac_ctrl_last, omitting digest_valid_reg: three assignments in the reset arm against two in the zeroize arm, measured by a census that counts assignments without naming which registers they target. That omission matters because :111-112 make both outputs of the module functions of that one register: tag is H2_digest when digest_valid_reg is set and zero otherwise, and tag_valid is the register itself. A zeroize therefore returns the FSM to idle while the module keeps asserting that it holds a valid tag.

The zeroize arm carries its own justification at :192-193, stating that digest_valid_reg is refreshed by the normal update path on a later cycle so it need not be touched. The same file contradicts that claim. The normal path at :202-203 writes the register only when digest_valid_we is raised; the FSM defaults that enable low at :329, and the CTRL_IDLE arm at :336-351 raises it only inside its next_cmd branch at :347, while the default arm clears it at :404. An engine sitting idle after a zeroize, which is precisely the post-zeroize state, never performs the promised refresh. A gate that strips comment lines before searching the arm is what separates the two facts: the register is named in that arm only inside the comment, never in code.

The same zeroize strobe is fanned out from this file to two child masked cores at :120 and :139. In src/sha512_masked/rtl/sha512_masked_core.sv the zeroize arm mirrors the reset arm register for register, 22 against 22, and clears its own digest_valid_reg at :316 exactly as its reset arm does at :290. The parent src/hmac/rtl/hmac.sv behaves the same way, 7 against 7, clearing tag_valid_reg in both arms at :204 and :214. Of the three modules on one strobe, only the audited one treats its validity flag as exempt.

Simulation of one unmodified hmac_core driven only through its ports confirms the behaviour: after a completed operation tag_valid=1 with tag[63:0]=6c2c68f7fb784420, and after a completed zeroize tag_valid=1 ready=1 with tag[63:0]=0000000000000000, still 1 after a further 200 idle cycles. Reproducing the parent's capture-enable expression from src/hmac/rtl/hmac.sv:163 against the real core output shows that enable re-asserting once after the zeroize, because the same strobe cleared the parent's own copy of the flag while the core kept its flag set.
detection_method: Located by CSBC, an LLM-driven analysis method that reasons over a single tree and reports register-transfer sites whose behaviour contradicts other arms of the same block, the block's own comments, the formulas of its consumers, or idioms repeated across sibling modules. The candidate here was raised as a state element cleared on reset but omitted from the zeroize arm of the same always_ff. It was then confirmed on its own evidence inside this tree: a scripted structural audit of the submitted sources (35 of 35 gates, result=PASS), a directed simulation of one unmodified hmac_core driven only through its ports (checks=6 fails=3 witness_hits=1, four covers at 1, result=PASS), and a negative control in which adding the single omitted assignment to a scratch copy flips the identical testbench (witness_hits=0, both defect covers at 0, tb_fails=0, one line added and none removed). No external repository, no other revision of this design, and no expected-answer list was consulted at any point.
security_impact: A zeroize is how software makes a cryptographic block safe to hand on, and this defect makes the block's answer to whether it holds a valid result untruthful across exactly that operation. Software polling HMAC512_STATUS.VALID after issuing a zeroize reads the valid bit still set and may take the all-zero TAG register as a completed authentication tag, turning a cleared block into a source of a fixed, attacker-predictable tag value. Separately and without any software polling, the parent's rising-edge tag capture at src/hmac/rtl/hmac.sv:163 fires after the zeroize, because that same strobe cleared the parent's own tag_valid_reg at :214 while the core kept its flag asserted; the parent then latches an all-zero tag into the software-readable TAG register at :227, after the TAG.hwclr at :267 had already cleared it. Both effects break the integrity of the block's reported results. No secret material is exposed: the child masked cores clear their own digests on the same strobe, which measurement confirms, so this is a false-completion and integrity defect rather than a disclosure one.
proposed_mitigation: Add the omitted clear to the zeroize arm of the reg_update block in src/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv, so the arm at :190-196 assigns digest_valid_reg <= 1'b0 alongside the two FSM registers, matching the reset arm at :185 and matching how the child sha512_masked_core:316 and the parent hmac.sv:214 write their own zeroize arms. This one line is exactly the negative control performed here, and it flips every violating check to passing while leaving both harness controls and the containment case intact.
Remove the comment at src/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv:192-193 with it, since the refresh it describes does not occur while the engine is idle and the comment is what makes the omission look deliberate.

As defence in depth, qualify the tag_valid output at src/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv:112 so no completion is reported unless the FSM has run to completion since the last clear, preventing any single missed assignment in a clear path from producing a false completion again.

Add an assertion that after a zeroize is taken, tag_valid stays low until the next command is issued, and extend the same check to every state element cleared by the reset arm of the same always_ff so the two arms cannot drift apart unnoticed.
exploit_or_attack_flow: Software at user level writes the HMAC block's key and message and starts an operation through HMAC512_CTRL at 0x10010010 (src/integration/rtl/caliptra_reg/caliptra_reg.h:979, block base 0x10010000 at :962). The operation completes and the core asserts tag_valid, measured as tag_valid=1 with tag[63:0]=6c2c68f7fb784420.

Software writes HMAC512_CTRL.ZEROIZE, bit 2 of that same register (src/integration/rtl/caliptra_reg/caliptra_reg.h:986-987). The field drives zeroize_reg at src/hmac/rtl/hmac.sv:259 and reaches the audited core at :171.

The core takes the zeroize arm at src/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv:190-196. The FSM returns to idle and the child masked cores clear their digests, but digest_valid_reg is not written, so tag_valid stays asserted. Measured as tag_valid=1 ready=1 tag[63:0]=0000000000000000 six cycles after the strobe.

The refresh promised by the comment at src/hmac/rtl/hmac_core.sv:192-193 never happens, because the FSM raises digest_valid_we only in the next_cmd branch at :347 and an idle engine issues no command. Measured as tag_valid still 1 after 200 further idle cycles.

Software polling HMAC512_STATUS at 0x10010018 reads VALID still set (src/integration/rtl/caliptra_reg/caliptra_reg.h:995, :1000-1001) and can read HMAC512_TAG_0 at 0x10010100 (:1195), taking a fixed all-zero value as a completed authentication tag.

Independently of any polling, the parent's capture enable at src/hmac/rtl/hmac.sv:163 sees core_tag_valid still high while its own tag_valid_reg was cleared by the same zeroize at :214, so it re-asserts and the parent latches the all-zero tag into the software-readable TAG register at :227, after the TAG.hwclr at :267 had already cleared it. Reproducing that expression against the real core output in the harness shows exactly one such edge after the zeroize.
